{"question": "Your team is building a dbt project with multiple core models in the models/core/activity_based_interest directory. You need to generate schema YAML documentation for all models in this folder and include column descriptions from upstream models where column names match. After generation, you want to validate the YAML syntax before publishing the documentation. Which approach should you use?", "options": ["Run dbt ls -m models/core/activity_based_interest --output name to list models, then invoke dbt run-operation generate_model_yaml with the model names and upstream_descriptions=True, followed by dbt docs generate", "Run dbt ls -m models/core/activity_based_interest --output name to list the models, then run dbt run to compile and materialize those models and finally run dbt docs generate to produce and validate schema documentation", "Run dbt run-operation generate_model_yaml -m models/core/activity_based_interest --args '{upstream_descriptions: True}' and then run dbt docs generate to build the docs", "Run dbt ls -m models/core/activity_based_interest --output name to list models, pass those names to dbt run-operation generate_model_yaml with upstream_descriptions=True to generate the .yml files, then run an external YAML linter (e.g., yamllint) on the generated files before running dbt docs generate"], "answer": "A", "answer_explanation": "The correct approach combines three key steps: (1) use dbt ls -m models/core/activity_based_interest --output name to programmatically list all model names in the directory, (2) invoke dbt run-operation generate_model_yaml with the collected model names and set upstream_descriptions=True to include matching column descriptions from upstream models, and (3) run dbt docs generate to validate YAML syntax before serving. This workflow ensures all models are captured, upstream descriptions are included where applicable, and syntax validation occurs before documentation is published.", "answer_text": "Run dbt ls -m models/core/activity_based_interest --output name to list models, then invoke dbt run-operation generate_model_yaml with the model names and upstream_descriptions=True, followed by dbt docs generate", "question_type": "SA", "summary_content": "The generate_model_yaml dbt macro creates schema YAML for one or more models. It requires the model_names parameter and optionally includes upstream column descriptions when upstream_descriptions=True (default is False). A single call can combine multiple model definitions into one .yml output.

Model names can be provided programmatically (for example, by piping the output of dbt ls) or listed explicitly. Documentation text can be stored in docs blocks using the {{% docs <name> %}} ... {{% enddocs %}} syntax and then referenced in generated schema YAML with the doc('<name>') function. After generating or editing YAML, run dbt docs generate to validate YAML syntax before serving docs.

Prefer adding new docs or docs blocks manually when adding new models or adding columns to existing models rather than fully automated replacements. Regex and command behavior may vary across platforms; verify outputs in your environment (examples were tested on Mac/VS Code).", "key_concepts": ["model_names is required when invoking generate_model_yaml.", "upstream_descriptions is optional and defaults to False; set it to True to include identical column names' descriptions from upstream models.", "A single generate_model_yaml call can output a combined .yml for multiple models.", "Create docs blocks with {{% docs <name> %}}...{{% enddocs %}} and reference them in schema YAML via {{ doc('<name>') }}.", "Run dbt docs generate to validate YAML and catch syntax errors before serving documentation."], "technical_details": "- model_names (required): supply one or more model names (string or list of strings).
- upstream_descriptions (optional, default=False): Boolean to include identical column names' descriptions from upstream models.
- To combine multiple models into one YAML, pass multiple names in model_names in a single call.
- Use dbt ls -m <path> --output name to list model names programmatically for piping into generate_model_yaml.
- After generating or editing YAML, run dbt docs generate to validate YAML syntax prior to running dbt docs serve.
- Add docs text using the docs block syntax: {{% docs <name> %}}...{{% enddocs %}} and reference it in schema YAML via {{ doc('<name>') }}.
- Prefer manual addition of docs/doc-blocks when adding models or columns to existing folders to avoid overwriting or incorrect replacements.
- Be aware that regex and shell behavior can vary by platform (the provided approach was tested on Mac/VS Code)."}

- Create mental models that stick

- Explain the specific challenge presented in the question using the analogy

{"question": "Your analytics team is building a dbt project with 12 models in the `staging` folder that should all be materialized as tables for performance reasons, while models in other folders remain as views. Currently, each model file contains a materialized: table declaration, creating redundant configuration across the project. What should you do to enforce consistent table materialization for the staging folder while reducing configuration overhead?", "options": ["Create an Airflow DAG that post-processes the staging models by running CTAS statements in the warehouse to convert the built views into tables after dbt runs", "Remove the materialized: table declarations from individual model files and configure folder-level materialization in dbt_project.yml for the staging folder", "Set the project-level default materialization to 'table' in dbt_project.yml so all models become tables, then add explicit 'materialized: view' overrides for the other folders that should remain views", "Implement a custom materialization macro that detects model file paths (or a staging tag) and forces those models to build as tables, then apply that custom materialization to models in the project (or set it as the default for affected models)."], "answer": "B", "answer_explanation": "Folder-level materialization in dbt_project.yml is the correct approach to enforce consistent materialization across multiple models while reducing redundancy. By configuring the materialization setting at the folder level in dbt_project.yml, all models in the staging folder automatically inherit the table materialization without requiring individual materialized: table declarations in each model file. This eliminates redundant per-model configuration and ensures consistency across the folder. Individual model files should have their redundant materialization declarations removed since the folder-level setting will apply to all models in that directory.", "answer_text": "Remove the materialized: table declarations from individual model files and configure folder-level materialization in dbt_project.yml for the staging folder", "question_type": "SA", "summary_content": "dbt models are materialized as views by default; explicitly declaring models as views is unnecessary. When a group of models in a folder should be tables instead of views, declare the materialization at the folder level in dbt_project.yml so all models in that folder inherit the table materialization and individual models do not each require a materialized: view or materialized: table line.

Incremental models require explicit incremental logic to behave correctly. Incremental models must use unique keys to deduplicate or merge incoming data and must use the is_incremental() macro to separate full-refresh behavior from incremental logic. Implementations should ensure that insert/update/delete logic that applies only on incremental runs is guarded by is_incremental() to avoid incorrect results on full-refresh runs.

Set folder-level materializations to reduce redundancy and enforce consistent materialization across multiple models, and always design incremental models with a unique key and is_incremental() guards to maintain correctness and idempotence.", "key_concepts": ["dbt models default to materialization 'view' — no explicit view declaration is required.", "Set folder-level materializations in dbt_project.yml to materialize all models in a folder as tables rather than adding per-model materialized settings.", "Incremental models must define unique keys and use the is_incremental() macro to separate incremental logic from full-refresh logic."], "technical_details": "- Default materialization: models are materialized as "view" by default; do not need to declare models as views.
- Folder-level materialization: define materialization for a folder in dbt_project.yml to materialize all models in that folder as tables (avoids per-model materialized: view or materialized: table entries).
- Incremental model requirements:
  - Define a unique key for the incremental model to support correct deduplication/merging behavior.
  - Use the is_incremental() macro to conditionally execute incremental-only SQL (separate from full-refresh SQL).
  - Ensure incremental logic uses the unique key to update or deduplicate rows during incremental runs."}

{"question": "Your dbt project contains 150 models organized into folders: staging, intermediate, and marts. Currently, you have tags applied to 80 models to support various selection workflows (daily runs, weekly aggregations, compliance checks). The team reports that maintaining these tags is becoming a significant overhead, and new models frequently miss the required tags. You need to reduce tagging maintenance while preserving the ability to run targeted model selections for different workflows.", "options": ["Use your CI pipeline to maintain lists of model names per workflow and invoke dbt run with explicit --models lists generated in the pipeline, removing all tags from models.", "Adopt a naming convention that prefixes model names with workflow labels (e.g., daily_, weekly_, compliance_) and run targeted jobs using dbt name/wildcard selectors (--models daily_*), leaving unprefixed models out of those workflows.", "Implement YAML selectors that define composable selection logic for each workflow without requiring tags on individual models, and keep most models untagged while reserving tags only for special cases that don't fit folder or YAML selector patterns.", "Add automation (a pre-commit hook or model generator) that injects workflow tags into new model files based on their folder or chosen template so developers no longer have to tag models manually."], "answer": "C", "answer_explanation": "YAML selectors enable intricate, layered selection logic that can replace complicated tagging schemes without requiring tags on every model. By implementing YAML selectors to define composable selection rules for daily runs, weekly aggregations, and compliance checks, the team can centrally manage selection logic rather than maintaining tags across 80 models. Keeping most models untagged minimizes maintenance overhead while reserving tags only for special cases that cannot be addressed through folder organization or YAML selector composition. This approach directly addresses the stated problem of tagging overhead while preserving targeted selection workflows.", "answer_text": "Implement YAML selectors that define composable selection logic for each workflow without requiring tags on individual models, and keep most models untagged while reserving tags only for special cases that don't fit folder or YAML selector patterns.", "question_type": "SA", "summary_content": "Prefer folder selectors or YAML selectors instead of tagging every model; the majority of a project’s models should remain untagged to reduce maintenance overhead. Organize models into folders when natural grouping exists so selectors can target groups without adding tags to each model.

Use YAML selectors for intricate, layered model selection to replace complicated tagging schemes. YAML selectors enable expressive, composable selection logic so teams can apply selection rules centrally rather than proliferating tags across many models.", "key_concepts": ["The majority of project models should remain untagged to minimize tagging overhead.", "Folder selectors can eliminate the need to tag every model in a folder by selecting models by location.", "YAML selectors enable intricate, layered selection logic and can replace complicated tagging schemes."], "technical_details": "- Keep most models untagged; reserve tags for a small set of special cases.
- Organize related models into folders so folder selectors can target them without per-model tags.
- Use folder selectors in cases where grouping by location or project structure is sufficient.
- Implement YAML selectors to express layered, composable selection rules that replace complex tag combinations.
- Prefer selector-based selection (folder or YAML) as the primary mechanism for model retrieval; apply tags only when a model requires special, individual identification."}

{"question": "Your analytics team is building a dbt project that will transform raw customer data into reporting tables. The team wants to reuse common data quality checks and utility macros across multiple models without maintaining duplicate code. Additionally, your organization plans to upgrade the dbt version across all environments next quarter, and you need a strategy to apply this upgrade consistently to the 40+ jobs running in dbt Cloud without manually editing each job configuration. What should you do?", "options": ["Install the dbt_utils package in your dbt_packages.yml file and configure the majority of your dbt Cloud jobs to inherit from the environment.", "Embed Great Expectations checks and their Python helper functions into each dbt model and then script individual dbt Cloud job updates through the REST API to pin and modify the dbt version for every job.", "Publish the shared macros as a private Python package (wheel) and install that dependency into each dbt Cloud job's Python environment, then pin every job to the target dbt version.", "Extract shared macros into a central ‘macro-only’ dbt project in your monorepo, reference it via a local path in each project's packages.yml, and update the monorepo's dbt config to roll out the new version."], "answer": "A", "answer_explanation": "Installing the dbt_utils package provides immediate access to community-maintained macros without duplicating code in your project, reducing maintenance overhead. Configuring the majority of jobs to inherit from the environment ensures that when you upgrade the dbt version at the environment level, those jobs automatically use the new version without requiring individual job edits. This approach scales efficiently across 40+ jobs and centralizes both shared logic and platform-level configuration management.", "answer_text": "Install the dbt_utils package in your dbt_packages.yml file and configure the majority of your dbt Cloud jobs to inherit from the environment.", "question_type": "SA", "summary_content": "Install the dbt_utils package to reuse community macros directly in your project so you do not need to copy macros into your codebase. Using the package provides immediate access to community-maintained macros and reduces duplication and maintenance overhead.

In dbt Cloud, configure jobs to inherit from the environment so upgrades to the environment-wide dbt version apply to those jobs without editing each job individually. Having the majority of jobs inherit from the environment makes version upgrades simpler and reduces per-job configuration work.

Apply both practices together: rely on community packages like dbt_utils to centralize shared logic and set jobs to inherit from the environment so platform-level changes (for example, updating the dbt version) propagate broadly and consistently.", "key_concepts": ["Install dbt_utils to access community macros without copying them into your project.", "dbt Cloud jobs can inherit from the environment so upgrades to the environment-wide dbt version affect those jobs.", "Making most jobs inherit from the environment simplifies version upgrades and reduces per-job configuration."], "technical_details": "- Install the dbt_utils package so macros are available in your project; copying macros into the project is not required.
- Verify that dbt Cloud jobs are configured to inherit from the environment to allow environment-level dbt version upgrades to apply to those jobs.
- Confirm the dbt version used by jobs and check whether the majority of jobs inherit from the environment to streamline future upgrades."}

{"question": "A data engineering team is building a dbt project to consolidate customer data from three separate source systems: a CRM platform, an ERP system, and a marketing automation tool. Each source contains customer identifiers, contact information, and transaction history in different formats and naming conventions. The team needs to ensure that data from each source is cleaned, standardized, and ready for downstream analytics models without creating fragile dependencies between sources. Which approach should the team implement?", "options": ["Create one staging model per source system that applies column renames, type normalization, and null handling, then orchestrate cross-source joins in Airflow tasks to produce the unified customer view", "Create one staging model per source system that applies column renames, type normalization, and null handling, then reference all three staging models in a downstream transformation model to perform cross-source joins", "Create a single staging model that ingests all three source systems, applies universal column renames, type normalization, and null handling, and performs the cross-source joins to produce a consolidated customer table", "Create one staging model per source system that applies column renames, type normalization, null handling, and also performs source-specific customer identity resolution and assigns a unified customer_id within each staging model"], "answer": "B", "answer_explanation": "The correct approach creates one staging model per source system, each applying source-specific cleaning and standardization (column renames, type normalization, null handling), then uses a downstream transformation model to reference and join all three staging models. This architecture isolates source-specific logic in staging models, prevents fragile cross-source dependencies, and keeps transformations simple and testable. Each staging model becomes a canonical, predictable view of its source that downstream models can safely consume. Cross-source joins belong only in higher-level transformation models explicitly designed to combine data across multiple sources, not within staging models themselves.", "answer_text": "Create one staging model per source system that applies column renames, type normalization, and null handling, then reference all three staging models in a downstream transformation model to perform cross-source joins", "question_type": "SA", "summary_content": "Every source must have a corresponding staging model that ingests the raw source and cleans and standardizes its structure. Staging models are the single place to apply column renames, type normalization, null handling, and minimal business-rule normalization for that source. Staging models should represent a normalized, predictable view of the source data for downstream models to consume.

Do not perform direct joins between different source systems inside staging models, and do not join other sources or intermediate models into a source's staging model. Downstream models should combine the standardized outputs of staging models rather than coupling sources together inside staging. This keeps source-specific logic isolated, prevents fragile cross-source dependencies, and makes testing and maintenance straightforward.

Enforce this constraint consistently: staging models remain simple, source-focused transformation layers. Complex cross-source logic belongs only in higher-level transformation models that explicitly reference multiple staging models and are designed for combining data across sources.", "key_concepts": ["One staging model per source: each source must have a dedicated staging model that standardizes its structure.", "Staging models perform cleaning and standardization only (renames, types, nulls, canonicalization), not cross-source joins.", "No direct joins between sources inside staging models; cross-source joins belong in downstream models that consume staging outputs.", "Isolating source logic in staging models reduces coupling, simplifies testing, and limits blast radius of source changes."], "technical_details": " - Create a single staging model for each raw source that: reads the raw table/view, applies column renames, enforces data types, handles nulls/malformed values, and outputs a standardized schema.
 - Do not include any joins to other sources or intermediate models inside a staging model; joins across data origins must occur only in downstream models that explicitly combine staging outputs.
 - Keep staging transformations idempotent and minimal (no complex aggregations or business-logic joins).
 - Downstream models should reference staging model outputs as canonical inputs for joins, aggregations, and business logic.

Models requiring managed permissions should declare grants as a dictionary (e.g., {'select': ['role']}), while models without dbt-managed permissions should set grants to {{}} to prevent dbt from managing them. Schema-level USAGE grants and database-specific advanced features like Snowflake row access policies are not first-class configurable objects in dbt and must be applied via post-hooks. This combination ensures selective permission management at the model level while enabling advanced policies through post-hooks.", "answer_text": "Configure grants as a dictionary (e.g., {'select': ['role']}) for models requiring managed permissions, set grants to {{}} for models without dbt-managed permissions, and use post-hooks to apply schema USAGE grants and row access policies", "question_type": "SA", "summary_content": "dbt Core v1.2 introduced a structured grants config that lets dbt manage object-level permissions for models and other resources. Grants are declared as a dictionary (for example, {'select': ['role']}) and dbt chooses the most efficient path to apply those grants rather than requiring manual SQL for every permission. If a resource has no grants config or it is set to {{ }}, dbt will not manage grants for that object.

When grants change, dbt computes the diff between the desired and current permissions and can emit REVOKE statements as part of the update process; these REVOKE statements are visible at debug log level. dbt knows whether existing grants should be "carried over" for incremental model runs based on the model's materialization and the target database. Grants are exposed in dbt metadata and the project graph, enabling macros to iterate graph.nodes to infer or aggregate schema-level grant information.

Schemas are not modeled as first-class configurable objects in dbt, so schema-level USAGE grants still need to be applied via hooks or post-hooks. Database-specific advanced permission features (for example, Snowflake row access policies or column masking policies) also require post-hooks to apply. The ability to manage grants is a global capability: users operating with the transformer role can change grants on any object as if they were the owner. - If grants is missing or set to {{ }}, dbt will not manage grants for that object
- dbt selects the most efficient SQL path to apply grants rather than requiring explicit SQL
- On grant changes, dbt computes diffs and may issue REVOKE statements; REVOKE activity appears in debug logs
- dbt determines whether to carry over existing grants for incremental models based on materialization type and the target database
- grants are available via dbt metadata/graph so macros can inspect graph.nodes to infer schema-level grant distributions
- Schema-level USAGE grants are not managed via the grants config and must be applied with hooks/post-hooks
- Database-specific features (e.g., Snowflake row access policies and column masking) require post-hooks to attach policies to objects
- Grant-management is global: a user with the transformer role can alter grants on any object as if they own it
- Use post-hooks to grant permissions to other transformers and BI users so collaborators retain access after model changes"}
